data.name: Krieg
data.detailed_description:
Built from the ground up for VR, Krieg is a team-based fantasy multiplayer competitive game.
Thrown into the middle of a war between The King's Army and The Ancients, only the strongest will survive. This war of epic mercenaries and guardians will decide the fate of the realm.

A major component unique to Krieg is the various character specific movement abilities. Krieg utilizes 3-dimensional space in a way no other VR competitive multiplayer has before.
Artificial locomotion has the ability to bring the most competitive experience possible for VR only titles. We fully embraced this and understand this might not be for everyone. Because of this Krieg will always have a free demo so there's no risk to try it.

The release only marks the beginning. Our focus is to build a community around the game by taking as much feedback as possible and implementing changes directly suggested from the players. We're confident we have made a very exciting and engaging game as our initial release but we are just as excited for the future to help define what a VR Esport can be.

reviews.review:
Krieg is a virtual reality multiplayer action game built around competitive combat, specialized characters, and unconventional movement. Rather than functioning as a traditional first-person shooter transplanted into VR, it attempts to make physical interaction and three-dimensional locomotion fundamental parts of the experience. The fantasy conflict between the King's Army and the Ancients provides the background for the battles, although story development is secondary to the competitive gameplay. The game was developed by Evan Davis, Bryce Davis, Gehrig Gosselin, and BOT Jungle Productions, with Castle Steps LLC and BOT Jungle Productions handling publishing duties.

One of Krieg's more interesting qualities is its character-based approach. Five playable characters were included in its Early Access content, with each designed around distinctive abilities and methods of moving through the environment. This creates more variety than simply handing everyone different weapons. Learning how a character navigates the battlefield is closely connected to learning how that character fights, giving movement a meaningful role in the overall skill system. Switching characters can therefore require players to reconsider positioning, mobility, and how they approach an opponent.

Artificial locomotion is an especially important part of the design. Krieg was created around the idea that VR players could become comfortable enough with artificial movement for developers to build faster and more mechanically demanding competitive experiences. This allows the game to move beyond stationary or teleportation-focused VR encounters. When everything works properly, maneuvering through an arena while using character abilities can produce an energetic style of combat that takes advantage of virtual reality rather than treating VR as little more than a different display method. The disadvantage is that players sensitive to artificial locomotion may experience discomfort, making Krieg less approachable for VR newcomers.

The content available in the Early Access version is considerably less ambitious than the core concept. There are five characters, an Ancient Ruins environment, and a Moving Capture Point mode. The objective encourages participants to remain mobile because control of the battlefield shifts as the capture point moves. This complements the character-specific locomotion mechanics quite well and discourages players from simply occupying one strong defensive location for an entire match. Unfortunately, having only one primary environment and mode severely restricts variety, particularly for a game intended to support repeated competitive sessions.

Krieg originally had much larger ambitions. Development plans included more characters, environments, competitive modes, balancing work, and cooperative content involving increasingly difficult AI opponents. Those additions could have turned the basic combat framework into a substantially broader multiplayer experience. However, the game has remained in Early Access for many years without the level of continued development required to fulfill that vision. As a result, it is better to judge Krieg according to what is actually available rather than what its roadmap once promised.

Its dependence on multiplayer also creates one of its largest modern limitations. A competitive game needs an active population for its mechanics to reach their full potential. Character abilities and specialized movement become far more interesting when they are being used against human opponents who understand the same systems. Without a healthy pool of players, the available content becomes significantly harder to appreciate. This makes Krieg an interesting example of how multiplayer VR projects can age differently from conventional single-player games, since even functioning mechanics cannot completely compensate for a limited community.

The presentation is functional rather than spectacular, with the fantasy setting mainly providing an identifiable backdrop for the action. Its greater appeal comes from experimenting with VR interaction and movement rather than visual extravagance. The game belongs to an earlier period of consumer VR when developers were actively exploring how room-scale movement, tracked controllers, artificial locomotion, and traditional competitive design could work together. Viewed from that perspective, some of its ideas remain intriguing even though the complete package feels unfinished.

Steam Deck compatibility is effectively unsupported for normal play. Krieg is a VR-only experience requiring a compatible virtual reality headset and tracked motion controllers, so the Steam Deck by itself cannot provide the hardware or control setup necessary to play the game as intended. Even if software compatibility could be achieved through SteamOS or Proton, the mandatory VR requirements make it unsuitable as a conventional handheld Steam Deck game.

Krieg ultimately feels more like an ambitious multiplayer VR experiment that never reached its full potential than a complete competitive release. Its specialized characters, unusual locomotion, physical interaction, and moving objective demonstrate some creative thinking about how VR multiplayer could differ from ordinary shooters. At the same time, the small amount of content, dependence on other players, prolonged Early Access status, and lack of continued development considerably reduce its long-term appeal. There is still something interesting here for VR enthusiasts curious about experimental competitive design from the earlier years of modern consumer VR, but expectations should remain firmly grounded in the game's limited state.

Krieg deserves credit for attempting a distinctive style of character-driven VR competition, but its promising mechanics are ultimately constrained by limited content, multiplayer dependence, and an Early Access vision that never developed into the larger experience it could have become.

Rating: 6/10
